tagline: Valley Pike towns give way to mountain gaps and mineral springs.
intro: US 11 links Shenandoah Valley towns along the historic Valley Pike route, with historical markers and scenic points along the road. A mountain branch, Orkney Grade, runs 12.63 miles between Mount Jackson and Orkney Springs. This two-lane Virginia Byway crosses Supin Lick Mountain and enters a narrow valley beneath Great North Mountain. Virginia’s byway designation identifies scenic roads that introduce travelers to alternative destinations.

The route through Woodstock carried earlier traffic under the names Great Wagon Road and Valley Pike; modern US 11 largely follows that older course. At Mount Jackson, the turnpike and water power from Mill Creek helped milling enterprises serve local farms. Another road, Howard’s Lick Turnpike, began there in 1856, heading toward mountainous western Virginia. In October 1864, fighting at Tom’s Brook and the ensuing Confederate retreat took place in significant part along the Valley Pike. US 11 now serves local traffic beside Interstate 81.

Travel south from Strasburg through Woodstock and Edinburg, where US 11 serves as Main Street. At Mount Jackson, Orkney Grade branches west through Mount Clifton toward Orkney Springs. Continue south on US 11 to New Market, another town where the through road becomes the main street.

moments.title: Edinburg Mill
moments.text: Edinburg Mill’s wooden upper stories rest on a limestone basement beside Stony Creek. The Grandstaff family built the present structure in 1848, replacing an 1813 complex that combined a sawmill, gristmill and carding operation. During the Civil War, Union troops under Philip Sheridan set the mill on fire as part of their scorched-earth campaign. Local women persuaded the soldiers to salvage the flour; the fire was extinguished and the building survived. Milling continued until 1978. Its deep roof forms a prominent gable above shed-roofed side extensions. The building uses older construction techniques, including shoulder posts.

moments.title: Fort Valley
moments.text: Passage Creek runs the length of Fort Valley, a 23-mile valley almost enclosed by the Massanutten ridges. Private farmland occupies much of the valley, while George Washington National Forest covers the surrounding slopes and ridges. At Elizabeth Furnace, ironmaking used Passage Creek for water power. The Civilian Conservation Corps built a recreation area on the site in 1936. Interpretive trails there explain the iron industry, while Camp Roosevelt provides another recreation area toward the valley’s southeastern end. At the northern end, Passage Creek escapes through a narrow gap beyond Elizabeth Furnace.

moments.title: Orkney Springs
moments.text: Mineral springs brought tourists to Orkney Springs, where private hotels on the former common green eventually became one hotel complex. Most of the original buildings survive, restored and in use. The Virginia House dates from the 1870s; the Maryland House dates from the mid-1850s but collapsed and was rebuilt after the Civil War. In 1979 the Episcopal Diocese of Virginia bought the hotel and incorporated it into Shrine Mont. The retreat center hosts conferences, summer camps and the annual Shenandoah Valley Music Festival. Its outdoor Cathedral Shrine of the Transfiguration is built of native stone.
